Export controls have historically been instruments for regulating things that can be counted, crated and inspected: centrifuges, machine tools, munitions. The Cold War regime coordinated through COCOM, and its successors such as the Wassenaar Arrangement, rested on a quiet premise, namely that the strategic value of a controlled technology resides in the artefact, so that interdicting its physical movement across a border is tantamount to interdicting the capability itself. Frontier artificial intelligence strains this premise almost to breaking point. A trained model is, physically, nothing more than a very large file of numerical weights, which can be copied at negligible cost and transmitted anywhere a network reaches. Yet its creation depends on inputs that are scarce, expensive and conspicuous: advanced semiconductors fabricated by a handful of firms, enormous quantities of electricity, and a small pool of specialist engineers. Control is therefore possible, but only at particular chokepoints, and policymakers have had to decide which of these to seize: the hardware on which models are trained, the weights that embody them, or the access through which they are used.

Since 2022, the United States has concentrated principally on the first chokepoint, restricting the sale of the most advanced chips and of the machinery used to make them. The rationale is one of denial and delay: if a rival cannot obtain the hardware, it cannot train comparable systems, or can do so only more slowly and at greater cost. Critics advance two objections. The first is that controls create precisely the incentive they are meant to remove: a state denied imports has every reason to subsidise domestic substitutes and to seek algorithmic efficiencies that economise on scarce hardware, so that restriction may hasten the self-reliance it seeks to prevent. The second is leakage, since chips diverted through third countries can undercut the whole design. Defenders reply that the objective was never permanent exclusion, and that in a competition where lead times matter, a delay of even a few months is itself a strategic gain.

The second chokepoint, the model weights, poses different difficulties. Unlike a chip, weights can be stolen, leaked or approximated through distillation, whereby a weaker model is trained on the outputs of a stronger one. A regime that guards the file but leaves the outputs freely queryable therefore controls less than it appears to; a regime that restricts queries, on the other hand, sacrifices the commercial openness on which the developers' revenues depend. The design problem is thus not simply how tightly to control but where, because every tightening at one point shifts pressure to another.

More recently, the locus of control has drifted up the stack, from hardware towards access. When, in June 2026, access to a pair of frontier models was suspended for under three weeks to comply with American export-control rules, and then restored once the controls were lifted, the episode illustrated something novel. A shipped machine, once delivered, cannot be recalled; a service can be withdrawn overnight from customers in dozens of jurisdictions, and reinstated just as quickly. Control over access is therefore continuous rather than one-off, and reversible rather than final. That reversibility makes it a more flexible instrument, but it also means that every customer's dependence is conditional on the policy of a third state. The restoration of service, far from dissolving the concern, arguably confirmed it: what had been demonstrated was not that the risk was small, but that it could be switched on and off at someone else's discretion.

Two rival prescriptions have emerged. The first, often described as sovereigntist, urges states to build domestic models and compute capacity and to treat them as infrastructure akin to a power grid. The difficulty is that the economics of frontier training favour concentration; a dozen national champions, each sub-scale and each dependent on imported chips, may deliver a sovereignty that is ostensible rather than real. The second, the interdependence view, holds that entanglement restrains weaponisation, much as commercial ties are said to have restrained great-power conflict. Yet this reasoning has a hidden condition. Mutual dependence deters only when each side stands to lose comparably from a rupture; where one party is the supplier and the other merely a customer, interdependence is a euphemism for exposure, and the party that can afford to withdraw is the one least deterred.

A further complication concerns the firms that operate the systems. Private developers are in effect the executors of public policy: they bear the commercial cost of compliance in lost revenue and eroded customer trust, but exercise no vote over the decisions that impose it. Foreign buyers, for their part, may respond by pricing in a regulatory risk premium, and some will conclude that a dependable but inferior local model is preferable to a superior one that might vanish. The perverse result is that measures which achieve a narrow security objective may lower the global market share of the very firms whose revenues finance the research on which security itself depends. Whether that constitutes a cost depends on how one ranks security against commercial leadership, and the two are not obviously separable. Nor is the problem purely commercial: governments and hospitals that embed foreign-hosted models in critical workflows acquire, without ever intending to, a supply-chain vulnerability of the kind that energy importers once discovered during oil embargoes.

Underlying the entire debate is an ambiguity in the word 'control'. It can mean denying a capability, delaying it, or retaining leverage over those who rely on it, and these aims call for different instruments and can work against one another. Denial encourages substitution; leverage requires that others depend on you, which requires that you not deny them; and the benefit of delay can never be observed directly, because it is measured against a counterfactual that does not occur. A policy that claims to secure all three simultaneously is likely to achieve none of them well. That the same instrument is defended in the language of security by some and attacked in the language of commerce by others suggests not confusion but a genuine plurality of goals, each legitimate, which no single instrument can fully serve. To ask whether export controls 'work' is thus to ask an under-specified question. The more revealing enquiry is which objective is being scored, over what horizon, and by whom.
questions.question: The author's description of the traditional export-control regime as resting on a 'quiet premise' implies which of the following?
options: A) Controls were originally designed for goods whose inspection was easy, and therefore they cannot be applied to any technology that is produced digitally.
B) The regime assumed that adversaries lacked the industrial base to build controlled items, an assumption that frontier AI has now falsified for all states.
C) The regime's tools were calibrated to controlled items whose value resides in discrete, traceable objects rather than replicable knowledge.
D) Cold War policymakers deliberately ignored the role of knowledge and labour in weapons production because knowledge could not be regulated at all.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Paragraph 1 states that the traditional regime assumed a technology's strategic value 'resides in the artefact', so that stopping physical movement equals stopping the capability. AI models are copyable files, straining this premise. Option C captures this artefact-versus-knowledge contrast cleanly without adding extreme claims like 'cannot be applied to any' or 'falsified for all states'.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the critics' contention (paragraph 2) that hardware controls hasten the self-reliance they aim to prevent?
options: A) Targeted states' domestic chip programmes were already expanding at a pace that the introduction of controls left essentially unchanged.
B) Firms in the targeted states have obtained restricted chips through intermediaries in third countries in quantities large enough to sustain training.
C) Algorithmic efficiency gains in targeted states have allowed comparable performance to be reached using a smaller quantity of less advanced hardware than before.
D) Defenders of the controls maintain that even short delays confer a strategic advantage in a race where lead times matter a great deal for outcomes.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The critics' claim is causal: controls accelerate domestic substitution. If domestic programs were expanding at the exact same pace prior to and after controls, then the controls did not accelerate substitution, severing the causal argument. Option B addresses leakage; Option C strengthens critics; Option D discusses delay objectives.

questions.question: The argument that controls could lower the market share of the controlling state's firms even as a security goal is achieved assumes that:
options: A) the controlling state's firms would be unable to serve foreign markets through regionalised deployments or contractual force majeure provisions.
B) security and commercial leadership are goals that cannot be pursued by the same state at the same time under any conditions.

The rise of cash transfers as an instrument of welfare is among the quieter revolutions of contemporary public policy. For much of the twentieth century, states that sought to help the poor preferred to provide goods: subsidised grain, fuel, fertiliser, housing. The reasoning was paternalist but not unreasonable. A household handed money might spend it on something other than food, and a state that wished to secure nutrition could best do so by distributing food. Cash transfers overturn this logic by trusting recipients to know their own needs, and they exploit a technological change, the spread of biometric identification, bank accounts and mobile payments, that has lowered the cost of moving money to individuals. In India, the combination of identity numbers, bank accounts and mobile phones, sometimes called the JAM trinity, has allowed subsidies once channelled through intermediaries to be paid directly into accounts, and in recent years a number of state governments have gone further, introducing unconditional monthly transfers to women that are defended as both welfare and empowerment.

Advocates of the shift advance three arguments. The first concerns leakage: in-kind systems lose commodities to diversion and pilferage, so that a rupee spent on grain does not deliver a rupee of grain, whereas money is traceable and passes through fewer hands. The second concerns choice: households differ in their needs, and a family with a sick child may rationally value medicine above a fifth kilogram of wheat. The third concerns market effects: cash spent locally supports small traders, whereas commodity distribution can displace them. Against the paternalist fear that recipients will squander transfers on temptation goods, advocates point to the balance of evidence from randomised trials in several countries, which suggests that such spending rarely rises.

Sceptics reply that the evidence is more equivocal than advocates imply. A fixed sum of money erodes with inflation, whereas a commodity entitlement delivers a physical quantity whatever the price, so that in a period of food-price spikes the cash recipient bears the price risk while the in-kind recipient is insured against it. Cash also presumes that functioning markets lie within reach; in remote areas with thin markets and few shops, money may not convert into the goods it was meant to buy. Finally, the value of a transfer depends on who controls it within the household, which explains the recent tilt towards women. That tilt rests on an empirical claim, that women on average spend more on children’s welfare, which holds on average but not universally, and policy built on an average inevitably misdescribes some households.

Cash transfers also have a political economy distinct from their economics. A subsidy embedded in an institution, such as a public distribution system, is hard to withdraw because it is tied to warehouses, transport and workers; a cash transfer is a line in a budget, which can be raised in an election year and quietly eroded in a lean one. Its visibility, money arriving with a message on a phone, makes it a potent electoral instrument, since the beneficiary can attribute the benefit directly to the government of the day. Critics conclude that cash transfers convert welfare into patronage by design. Defenders answer that the same visibility improves accountability: a beneficiary who receives less than was promised knows it at once, whereas the recipient of adulterated grain often cannot tell.

A more structural concern is that cash and public provision are not substitutes at all, because they draw on the same fiscal envelope. A state that commits a growing share of its budget to recurring transfers has less to spend on schools, clinics, roads and sanitation, goods whose benefits are collective and which markets do not readily supply. A woman with a transfer can buy medicines but cannot buy a functioning primary health centre; a household can purchase tuition but not a school system. The question, on this view, is not cash versus kind but cash versus capital: whether recurring transfers displace investment whose returns accrue over decades. Defenders object that the dichotomy is false, since transfers may be financed by removing inefficient subsidies rather than by cutting investment. Sceptics respond that in practice the ratchet turns one way, because a transfer, once announced, is politically irreversible, while a deferred investment is invisible until the day it is missed.

Increasingly, therefore, the debate has moved from whether to transfer cash to how a transfer should be designed. Targeting reduces cost but raises exclusion errors, in which deserving households are left out, sometimes through a mismatch of records rather than any real ineligibility. Conditionality, such as requiring children to attend school, can improve outcomes but demands administrative capacity and may penalise the poorest, who find conditions hardest to meet. Indexation protects real value but enlarges the fiscal commitment. Each choice trades one virtue for another; there is no configuration that is simultaneously cheap, inclusive and inflation-proof, and the claim that one exists is usually a sign that its costs have been moved out of sight.

What is at stake, then, is less a technical choice than a view of the state. To advocate cash is to claim that the state’s comparative advantage lies in finance and payments rather than in running supply chains; to defend provision is to claim that the state’s distinctive function is to supply what neither markets nor households can. Both are claims about the limits of state capacity, and they diverge because they locate those limits differently: advocates of cash tend to assume that the state is better at paying than at delivering, sceptics that it is better at building than at sustaining fiscal restraint. Evidence can narrow the disagreement but is unlikely to end it, since capacity itself varies across regions and across time, and what is true of one administration in one decade may not hold for another.

For more than a century, photographs and sound recordings have enjoyed a special standing as evidence. A court will admit a photograph more readily than a description of the same scene, and a recorded confession carries a weight that a recollection of one does not. This standing has never rested on the impossibility of forgery: darkroom retouching, staged tableaux and spliced tape were all familiar by the early twentieth century. It rested instead on the cost of forgery. Faking a convincing image required skill, time and equipment, and the result usually left traces that an expert could find. Trust was therefore a rational default, because deception was expensive and the expected number of forgeries was small. The authority of a medium, on this account, is an economic fact as much as a technical one, and it can vanish when the economics change. Generative artificial intelligence has changed them abruptly. A convincing clone of a voice, or a video of a person saying words they never said, can now be produced in minutes by someone with no specialist training and almost no money.

The obvious fear is deception: a fabricated clip of a candidate released on the eve of an election, a cloned voice instructing an employee to transfer funds. These dangers are real, and frauds using cloned voices have already been reported. Yet research on misinformation suggests that the relationship between the realism of a fake and its persuasive effect is weaker than intuition suggests. The most widely shared falsehoods have often been 'cheap fakes': authentic footage relabelled with a false caption, or a genuine clip slowed down or cropped. Such material requires no technical sophistication, and its reach depends less on how convincing it is than on whether it tells audiences what they are already inclined to believe and on whether platforms circulate it. If so, the binding constraints on harm are demand and distribution rather than production, and cheapening production further may matter less than alarmed commentary assumes.

A quieter danger follows from the very awareness that such commentary has spread. The legal scholars Robert Chesney and Danielle Citron have named it the liar’s dividend: once the public knows that recordings can be fabricated, anyone caught on a genuine recording gains a new defence, namely that it is a fake. The defence does not require that any deepfake exist, nor that the claim be plausible; it requires only that the audience consider fabrication possible and be unable to check. The harm therefore resides in a belief about what is possible, not in any artefact. This has an uncomfortable implication for the remedy most often proposed, public education. Campaigns that teach people that anything might be fake risk producing not sharper scepticism but indiscriminate doubt, and indiscriminate doubt is exactly the condition in which the liar’s dividend pays best. Teaching people to doubt is not the same as teaching them to doubt well.

Technical responses fall into two families. Detection tools try to recognise the statistical fingerprints of generated content. They face an arms race, since a detector trained on one generation of generators tends to fail against the next, and their errors are costly in both directions: a missed fake deceives, but a genuine recording wrongly flagged hands the liar a fresh exhibit. Provenance schemes take the opposite approach. Rather than asking whether a file is fake, they ask whether it can be shown to be authentic, by cryptographically signing images at the moment of capture and recording each later edit, as industry coalitions developing 'content credentials' propose. The attraction is that verification replaces guesswork. The weakness is that such schemes are voluntary and partial. Much genuine footage, including archival material, recordings on basic phones and screenshots, will lack credentials, and metadata is often stripped as files pass through platforms. The absence of a credential, therefore, proves nothing, and a system that can certify some truths cannot by itself refute any falsehood.

Institutions with resources, such as news agencies, governments and large companies, can adopt provenance practices, train staff to use them and defend their records in court. Laws against election deepfakes can be invoked to suppress satire and legitimate criticism by branding it fabricated. The obvious fear is deception: a fabricated clip of a candidate released on the eve of an election, a cloned voice instructing an employee to transfer funds. These dangers are real, and frauds using cloned voices have already been reported. Yet research on misinformation suggests that the relationship between the realism of a fake and its persuasive effect is weaker than intuition suggests. The most widely shared falsehoods have often been 'cheap fakes': authentic footage relabelled with a false caption, or a genuine clip slowed down or cropped. Such material requires no technical sophistication, and its reach depends less on how convincing it is than on whether it tells audiences what they are already inclined to believe and on whether platforms circulate it. If so, the binding constraints on harm are demand and distribution rather than production, and cheapening production further may matter less than alarmed commentary assumes.

A quieter danger follows from the very awareness that such commentary has spread. The legal scholars Robert Chesney and Danielle Citron have named it the liar’s dividend: once the public knows that recordings can be fabricated, anyone caught on a genuine recording gains a new defence, namely that it is a fake. The defence does not require that any deepfake exist, nor that the claim be plausible; it requires only that the audience consider fabrication possible and be unable to check. The harm therefore resides in a belief about what is possible, not in any artefact. This has an uncomfortable implication for the remedy most often proposed, public education. Campaigns that teach people that anything might be fake risk producing not sharper scepticism but indiscriminate doubt, and indiscriminate doubt is exactly the condition in which the liar’s dividend pays best. Teaching people to doubt is not the same as teaching them to doubt well.

Technical responses fall into two families. Detection tools try to recognise the statistical fingerprints of generated content. They face an arms race, since a detector trained on one generation of generators tends to fail against the next, and their errors are costly in both directions: a missed fake deceives, but a genuine recording wrongly flagged hands the liar a fresh exhibit. Provenance schemes take the opposite approach. Rather than asking whether a file is fake, they ask whether it can be shown to be authentic, by cryptographically signing images at the moment of capture and recording each later edit, as industry coalitions developing 'content credentials' propose. The attraction is that verification replaces guesswork. The weakness is that such schemes are voluntary and partial. Much genuine footage, including archival material, recordings on basic phones and screenshots, will lack credentials, and metadata is often stripped as files pass through platforms. The absence of a credential, therefore, proves nothing, and a system that can certify some truths cannot by itself refute any falsehood.

The distributional consequences deserve more attention than they have received. Institutions with resources, such as news agencies, governments and large companies, can adopt provenance practices, train staff to use them and defend their records in court. The citizen who films an incident of police violence, or a village that records an illegal clearing of forest, typically cannot. Such witnesses have historically relied on the credibility of the medium itself, since a video needs no institutional backing to carry force. If credentialed footage becomes the norm, footage without credentials may be treated as suspect, and those with least institutional power would lose the evidentiary standing on which they most depend. A safeguard designed to protect truth could thus end up protecting the powerful, who are best placed to certify their own version of events and to cast doubt on everyone else’s.

Regulation faces its own difficulties. Mandatory labelling of synthetic content is easy to state but hard to enforce across borders against anonymous publishers, and a false clip can circle the globe before a court has convened. Laws against election deepfakes can be invoked to suppress satire and legitimate criticism by branding it fabricated. Labelling also has a subtle perverse effect, documented in experiments on fact-checking: when only some false content is flagged, unflagged content is often presumed to be authentic, an 'implied truth effect'. A regime that labels what it can detect may thereby lend credibility to whatever it fails to detect, which will, by construction, be the most sophisticated fakes.

It would be wrong to conclude that nothing can any longer be believed. Synthetic media does not so much create falsehood, which has always been abundant, as alter the price of evidence: what was once cheap to trust has become expensive to verify. Societies have met similar shifts before. The printing press, which multiplied forged documents as readily as genuine ones, eventually produced citation practices, editors, archives and courts of record, institutions whose function was to vouch. The likely trajectory is that belief will migrate from the recording itself to the institutions that stand behind it. Whether those institutions turn out to be plural and accountable, or concentrated and opaque, is the question that matters. Technology determines the cost of forgery; politics will determine who bears the cost of verification.
questions.question: The argument that provenance schemes could disadvantage citizen witnesses assumes that:
options: A) citizen footage is more likely to be fabricated than footage produced by news agencies and other well-resourced institutions in general
B) institutions would deliberately refuse to certify material submitted by members of the public who have no formal standing or affiliation
C) platforms strip metadata from uploaded files in order to prevent citizens from proving that their recordings are authentic in disputes
D) footage lacking credentials would be treated with greater suspicion once credentialed footage becomes the norm
questions.explanation: Explanation: Paragraph 5 asserts that if credentialed media becomes standard, uncredentialed raw footage will be viewed with skepticism, stripping power from citizens lacking cryptographic capture infrastructure.

questions.question: Which of the following best captures the author’s concluding view?
options: A) Belief will likely migrate from recordings to vouching institutions, so the character of those institutions becomes decisive.
B) Synthetic media has made all evidence worthless, and societies must learn to live without any reliable way of settling factual disputes.
C) Technical safeguards such as provenance and detection will eventually restore the old trust in recordings, making institutional vouching unnecessary.
D) Synthetic media creates falsehood on a scale previously unknown, which is why regulation of publishers is now the only adequate response.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Paragraph 7 explicitly states that belief will migrate from isolated recordings to mediating vouching institutions, making the accountability of these institutions the primary socio-political question.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. That assumption, however, ignores the subtle ways in which structural inequality limits choice before a decision is ever made.
2. Standard economic theory models individuals as autonomous agents evaluating choices freely.
3. When opportunity sets are constrained by caste or poverty, freedom of choice becomes an abstract fiction.
4. Policy intervention must therefore address initial conditions rather than merely protecting formal choice.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 sets up the baseline assumption of standard theory (autonomous agents). 1 introduces the counter-argument via 'That assumption'. 3 elaborates on how poverty/caste constrains opportunity. 4 ('therefore') delivers the logical policy conclusion.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Central banks responded by dramatically raising interest rates to suppress aggregate demand.
2. The post-pandemic inflationary spike was triggered primarily by severe global supply-chain bottlenecks.
3. This policy choice risked triggering recessions to cure an inflation that was not demand-driven.
4. Raising rates reduces borrowing but does nothing to clear congested container ports or restore grain exports.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 identifies supply bottlenecks as the primary cause of inflation. 1 states the central bank response (raising rates). 4 explains the mismatch between interest rates and physical supply chains. 3 ('This policy choice') summarizes the resulting structural risk.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. In a digital economy, however, raw data is continuously extracted without immediate compensation.
2. Classical property rights were designed to protect physical assets that could be exclusively possessed.
3. This asymmetry allows tech platforms to capture immense economic rents while generating minimal local employment.
4. Data, once copied, can be exploited by platforms simultaneously without depleting the original file.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 establishes classical property rights over physical assets. 1 contrasts this with digital data extraction ('however'). 4 explains the non-depletable nature of data files. 3 ('This asymmetry') derives the economic rent consequence.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Over time, those micro-decisions aggregate into major ecological degradation.
2. The tragedy of the commons arises when individuals act rationally in their short-term self-interest.
3. Each farmer adds one more cow to the shared pasture, capturing full private benefit while diluting public cost.
4. Without collective institutions or clear property rules, mutual ruin becomes mathematically inevitable.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 defines the concept (tragedy of the commons). 3 provides the classic pasture illustration. 1 traces the cumulative aggregation into ecological damage. 4 completes the logical arc by concluding mutual ruin.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. This loss of genetic diversity leaves crop monocultures hyper-vulnerable to novel pathogens.
2. Modern industrial agriculture prioritizes a tiny fraction of high-yielding crop varieties.
3. A single fungus could consequently wipe out a massive share of the global harvest overnight.
4. Thousands of traditional landrace seeds have been abandoned across the developing world.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 states the agricultural priority (high-yielding varieties). 4 provides the direct consequence (abandonment of landrace seeds). 1 ('This loss of genetic diversity') links the structural vulnerability. 3 ('consequently') details the ultimate catastrophic outcome.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Modern AI models are often hailed as neutral engines of objective truth. However, because these systems are trained on historical text corpora generated by biased human societies, they systematically reproduce existing socio-economic inequalities. The statistical patterns extracted by machine learning algorithms reflect historical discrimination rather than universal logic. When these models are deployed to automate hiring, loan approvals, or judicial sentencing, they do not eliminate human bias; they codify and scale it under a veneer of mathematical objectivity.'
options: A) AI hiring and judicial algorithms should be banned globally because machine learning relies on flawed historical text corpora.
B) Machine learning models are flawed because software engineers intentionally code discriminatory rules into neural networks.
C) AI systems automate human bias by disguising historical societal inequities in training data as objective statistical patterns.
D) Deploying AI models in banking and law eliminates human subjectivity and ensures perfectly fair allocation.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph's core point is that AI models encode historical societal prejudice into automated decisions behind mathematical neutrality. Option C summarizes this accurately. Option A is an overreaching policy ban; Option B falsely alleges intentional coding by engineers; Option D states the exact opposite of the paragraph.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'In classical democratic theory, public policy is forged through reasoned debate among informed citizens. In practice, however, voter attention is a scarce resource exploited by political campaign strategists. Rather than engaging in substantive policy debates, campaigns increasingly deploy targeted emotional outrage to mobilize voters. Polarization is thus not an accidental byproduct of modern media; it is a deliberate, economically rational strategy for maximizing voter turnout and digital engagement.'
options: A) Political polarization is a calculated strategy exploiting emotional outrage to drive engagement, contradicting classical democratic ideals.
B) Voters are inherently irrational and incapable of understanding complex public policy debates during election cycles.
C) Modern media platforms are solely responsible for political division because they ban substantive debate on public policy.
D) Turnout increases only when political campaigns focus strictly on objective economic facts rather than emotional appeals.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph argues that polarization is a deliberate strategy using outrage to capture scarce attention. Option A captures both the contrast with classical theory and the strategic driver. Option B blames voter intellect; Option C uses 'solely responsible'; Option D contradicts the passage.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'Scientific progress is widely assumed to be a smooth, cumulative accumulation of facts. However, Thomas Kuhn argued that science develops through long periods of relative stability interrupted by sudden revolutionary paradigm shifts. During stable 'normal science', researchers work within accepted frameworks, ignoring minor anomalies. Only when anomalies accumulate to a critical threshold does the existing paradigm collapse, forcing the scientific community to adopt a fundamentally new worldview.'
options: A) Kuhn proved that scientific research is unscientific because researchers routinely ignore empirical facts during normal science.
B) Scientific development proceeds not linearly, but through stable periods punctuated by paradigm shifts triggered by accumulated anomalies.
C) Paradigm shifts occur continuously in science because researchers actively search for anomalies to overthrow existing frameworks.
D) Cumulative accumulation of facts is the only reliable method for establishing objective scientific truth across disciplines.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Option B captures Kuhn's model cleanly: non-linear progress, normal science stability, and crisis via accumulated anomalies leading to paradigm shifts.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'In competitive markets, price signals coordinate production by communicating consumer demand to producers. When governments impose artificial price ceilings on essential commodities like bread or housing, prices can no longer rise to signal scarcity. As a result, consumer demand rises while producer incentive to supply falls, making ________.'
options: A) production rise rapidly to meet the expanded purchasing power of poorer consumers in urban areas
B) shortages and informal black markets an inevitable structural outcome of the policy
C) government price controls the most effective long-term instrument for eliminating poverty
D) producers completely immune to cost changes in raw material markets
questions.explanation: Explanation: When demand rises while supply falls due to price ceilings, physical shortages are guaranteed, giving rise to black markets. Option B completes the economic logic.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'Intellectual property rights are granted on the assumption that temporary monopolies incentivize innovation by allowing inventors to recoup research costs. However, when patents are granted on overly broad or foundational discoveries, they allow patent holders to block follow-on researchers. Instead of fostering innovation, overly permissive patent regimes ________.'
options: A) guarantee that all downstream technologies become completely free and accessible to the public
B) stifle subsequent technological progress by erecting legal tolls across essential research pathways
C) eliminate all corporate profits in pharmaceutical and biotechnology sectors overnight
D) force governments to nationalize private research labs during economic downturns
questions.explanation: Explanation: Blocking follow-on researchers creates a bottleneck, turning patents into barriers to innovation. Option B logically completes this contrast.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'PERNICIOUS':
options: A) Insidious
B) Salubrious
C) Innocuous
D) Anodyne
questions.explanation: Explanation: Pernicious means highly harmful or destructive, especially in a subtle or gradual manner; 'insidious' is its closest synonym. 'Salubrious' (healthful), 'innocuous' (harmless), and 'anodyne' (bland/harmless) are antonyms.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'SANGUINE':
options: A) Optimistic
B) Despondent
C) Buoyant
D) Confident
questions.explanation: Explanation: Sanguine means cheerfully optimistic; 'despondent' (feeling profound hopelessness) is its antonym.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'OBFUSCATE':
options: A) Elucidate
B) Cloud
C) Explicate
D) Unravel
questions.explanation: Explanation: Obfuscate means to deliberately render obscure or unclear; 'cloud' is its synonym. The other options mean to clarify.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'FASTIDIOUS':
options: A) Meticulous
B) Punctilious
C) Cursory
D) Scrupulous
questions.explanation: Explanation: Fastidious means excessively particular, attentive to detail; 'cursory' (hasty and superficial) is its antonym.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'INCHOATE':
options: A) Formative
B) Explicit
C) Articulate
D) Consummate
questions.explanation: Explanation: Inchoate means just begun and not fully formed; 'formative' or rudimentary matches this meaning.

questions.question:
Choose the correct word to fill in the blank:
'The minister's ________ response, delivered during a heated parliamentary debate, only intensified public suspicion that the government was concealing critical audit findings.'
options: A) candid
B) unequivocal
C) equivocal
D) forthright
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Equivocal' means ambiguous or intentionally misleading, which logically triggers suspicion of concealment.

questions.question:
Choose the pair that best fills the blanks:
'While the executive hailed the merger as a ________ triumph, industry analysts cautioned that its long-term benefits remained purely ________.'
options: A) minor; substantial
B) monumental; illusory
C) disastrous; verified
D) negligible; tangible
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'While' signals contrast between the executive's praise ('monumental') and analysts' skepticism ('illusory').

questions.question: Select the option that correctly explains the meaning of the idiom 'To cut the Gordian knot':
options: A) To perpetuate a bureaucratic debate indefinitely
B) To solve a complex problem through bold, decisive action
C) To make a minor error that ruins a delicate consensus
D) To surrender unconditionally to an adversary
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Cutting the Gordian knot' refers to taking swift, decisive action to resolve an apparently intractable problem.

questions.question: Select the sentence in which the word 'COMPLAYSANT' (or 'COMPLAISANT') is used correctly:
options: A) The complaisant auditor refused to sign the financial statements due to blatant regulatory discrepancies.
B) He remained complaisant about his exam preparation despite failing two diagnostic mock tests.
C) The complaisant assistant eagerly agreed to every modification requested by the demanding director.
D) She issued a complaisant complaint regarding the late arrival of the express train.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Complaisant' means eager to please, obliging, or agreeable. Option C uses it correctly. (Confusing it with 'complacent'—smug/self-satisfied—is a classic error shown in Option B).

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'Neither the lead investigator nor the junior analysts ________ able to locate the corrupted files on the server.'
options: A) was
B) were
C) is being
D) has been
questions.explanation: Explanation: When subjects are connected by 'neither... nor', the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. 'Junior analysts' is plural, so 'were' is correct.

questions.question:
Spot the error in the following sentence:
'Hardly had the chairman (A) / finished his opening remarks (B) / than the dissenting shareholders (C) / began shouting slogans (D).'
options: A) Hardly had the chairman
B) finished his opening remarks
C) than the dissenting shareholders
D) began shouting slogans
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Hardly... when' is the correct correlative conjunction pair. Replacing 'than' with 'when' corrects the sentence ('than' is paired with 'No sooner').

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
options: A) Walking through the ancient ruins, several intact marble statues were discovered by the archeologists.
B) Walking through the ancient ruins, the archeologists discovered several intact marble statues.
C) While walking through the ancient ruins, several intact marble statues appeared to the archeologists.
D) Having walked through the ancient ruins, several intact marble statues were seen.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Options A, C, and D contain misplaced/dangling modifiers (making the statues walk). Option B correctly places 'the archeologists' as the subject performing the action 'walking'.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'The board demanded that the chief executive ________ an immediate explanation for the fiscal deficit.'
options: A) provides
B) provide
C) provided
D) should have provided
questions.explanation: Explanation: Verbs of demand, command, or recommendation (demand, insist, suggest) require the subjunctive mood (base form of the verb without '-s'). Thus, 'provide' is correct.

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
options: A) She is one of those rare officers who acts with absolute integrity in every crisis.
B) She is one of those rare officers who act with absolute integrity in every crisis.
C) She is one of those rare officer who act with absolute integrity in every crisis.
D) She is a officer who act with absolute integrity in every crisis.
questions.explanation: Explanation: In the structure 'one of those [plural noun] who [verb]', the relative pronoun 'who' refers to the plural noun 'officers', requiring a plural verb 'act'.

questions.question:
Spot the error in the sentence:
'The economic conditions (A) / are much more worse (B) / than the central bank (C) / projected last quarter (D).'
options: A) The economic conditions
B) are much more worse
C) than the central bank
D) projected last quarter
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Worse' is already comparative. Using 'more worse' is a double comparative error. It should be 'much worse'.

questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
'The corporate restructuring plan was deemed entirely compatible ________ existing labor regulations.'
options: A) to
B) with
C) for
D) towards
questions.explanation: Explanation: The adjective 'compatible' takes the preposition 'with'.

questions.question: Identify the grammatically INCORRECT sentence:
options: A) Scarcely had she stepped out of the house when it began to rain heavily.
B) Neither of the two proposals presented by the consultants is acceptable to the board.
C) The committee have submitted its final report to the ministry yesterday.
D) If he had studied more systematically, he would have cleared the examination easily.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'The committee' taking the singular pronoun 'its' must agree in number with a singular verb ('has submitted'). Furthermore, the definite past time marker 'yesterday' requires simple past ('submitted') rather than present perfect.
